Teach in three quick clusters. Students need their Unit Vocabulary graphic organizers."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Cluster 1: resented and regretted. Write both words. Say: Both begin with re-. In redo, re- means again and can be peeled off. Here the re- is part of the word's root, so we use the sentence around each word on p. 39 to decide the meaning. Both words look back at something that already happened."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Using the sentences on p. 39, how are resented and regretted different?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Resented means feeling angry or bitter about something unfair. Regretted means feeling sorry about something that happened or something you did. Resent is anger, regret is being sorry."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Cluster 2: routine, suckered, rebellious, desperate. Have students find each word on its page and underline clues. For routine, look for clues about things done the same way over and over. For suckered, ask whether it sounds formal or like how kids really talk; that informal tone helps build Percy's voice. For rebellious, notice the root rebel and the suffix -ious, meaning full of or having the quality of. For desperate on p. 42, ask what the situation shows about how few options the characters have."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What clues help you figure out what rebellious means?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The word rebel is inside it, and a rebel goes against rules. So rebellious means acting against rules and the people in charge."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Cluster 3: muzzle, bellow, cloven, hooves. Write bellow and hooves. In bellow, the letters ow make the long o sound. In hooves, the letters oo make the sound in moon. Have students say each word twice. Then connect meanings: a muzzle is an animal's nose and mouth, cloven means split in two, hooves are an animal's hard feet."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which words in this cluster help you picture a creature, and what do they tell you?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Muzzle, cloven and hooves all make me picture an animal. Cloven hooves are split in two like a goat's. Bellow tells me something is loud and deep, so the creature is big and scary."},{"type":"directions","text":"Add all ten words to your Unit Vocabulary graphic organizer. For each word, write the page number, a definition in your own words, and one clue from the text. Underline the vowel team in bellow and hooves. Circle the prefix re- in resented and regretted."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Words like suckered and bellow are informal or vivid. Point out that Riordan's word choices give Percy's narration a real, kid-like voice. This prepares students for RL.6.4 and L.6.5 work later in the unit."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Using context to determine word meaning","tryThis":"Have students read the whole sentence aloud, cover the word, and say what would make sense in the blank. Offer two choices and ask which fits. Provide the frame: I think ___ means ___ because the text says ___."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: Word choice","tryThis":"Ask students to compare desperate with a milder word such as worried and explain how the stronger word changes the mood. Have them find one more word in pp. 37–43 that shows Percy's voice."}]}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Part A: Students reread pp. 37–43 and cite key events and reactions to track the turning point. Part B: Students explain how this episode closes Percy's ordinary world and launches the adventure, connecting it to fears and values about family.","activities":[{"id":"lia-track-turning-point","title":"Part A: Track the Turning Point","minutes":15,"standards":["RL.6.1","L.6.4"],"routine":"Close Read and Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief","pages":"pp. 37–43"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Today we read the storm, the monster attack and Grover's reveal as one chain of events. Our job is to find the exact moments where things change and cite them. A strong citation says what the text says and explains what it shows."},{"type":"directions","text":"Reread pp. 37–43 and complete a three-column chart. Column 1: Key event (the storm, the monster attack, Grover's reveal). Column 2: Evidence (a short quote or paraphrase with the page number). Column 3: Reaction (how Percy, Grover or others respond, and what that shows). Put a star next to the moment you think is the turning point."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Page numbers vary by edition. If students' copies differ slightly, have them cite the pages in their own books and keep the focus on the three events."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Early in these pages, what details show Percy's usual routine, and what signs show it is about to break?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"At the start, things look like a normal day with Percy's usual kind of trouble. Then the storm and strange behavior around him are warning signs that his ordinary world is about to break."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How do Percy and Grover react during the monster attack? Cite a detail."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The text shows them acting desperate, and the creature's bellow shows how big and dangerous it is. Percy doesn't just freeze. He tries to protect Grover, which shows he is braver than he thinks."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does Grover's reveal on p. 43 show, and why does it change Percy's world?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The cloven hooves show Grover isn't a normal kid. He was hiding the truth, so Percy learns the people he trusted aren't what they seemed. His ordinary world isn't real anymore."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What fears and values about family show up on these pages?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy is afraid of losing the people he cares about, and he values protecting them, like Grover and his mom. That shows family matters to him even when he is scared."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in reading closely and citing evidence about events and reactions. Language focus: precise reaction verbs and sequence words.","sayAsk":"Have students say each event aloud to a partner before writing it. Ask: What happens first? Then what? How does Percy react? Frames: First, ___ happens on page ___. Percy reacts by ___. This shows that ___. Rephrase short answers: You said Percy was scared. We can say, Percy reacts fearfully when the creature bellows.","watchFor":"If students retell the whole story without citing, then prompt: Which exact line shows that? Give me the page number. If students list events without reactions, then prompt: How did the character respond? Have students find and copy the matching line, then complete: On page ___, the text says ___, which shows ___."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: Choosing the strongest evidence","tryThis":"Ask students to rank the three events by how much each changes Percy's life and defend the ranking with two quotes. Have them decide whether the turning point is one moment or a chain of moments."}]}]},{"id":"lia-explain-plot-structure","title":"Part B: Explain the Turning Point in the Plot Structure","minutes":15,"standards":["RL.6.5","RL.6.1"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief","pages":"pp. 37–43"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"A plot has parts: exposition (the ordinary world and characters), rising action (problems build), the climax or turning point (the big change), and what follows. Each chapter does a job in that structure. The earlier chapters showed Percy's ordinary world and its troubles. This episode has a new job: it closes that world and launches the adventure. To explain it, say what came before, what changes, and what it makes possible."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Model: In pp. 37–43, the storm, the monster attack and Grover's reveal work together as a turning point. Before this episode, Percy's world is school troubles and a hard home life. Because the creature attacks and Grover's cloven hooves are revealed, Percy learns that things he thought were impossible are real. As a result, he cannot go back to normal, and the adventure begins."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does Percy's ordinary world look like before this episode, and how do you know?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Before this, Percy gets in trouble at school and worries about his mom and Gabe. The earlier chapters show normal problems, not monsters."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does this episode launch the adventure? What can Percy no longer do?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy now knows the truth is bigger than he believed, so he can't pretend everything is normal. He has to move forward into something new."},{"type":"directions","text":"Write a 4–5 sentence paragraph explaining how the storm, the monster attack and Grover's reveal close Percy's ordinary world and launch the adventure. Use at least two cited details from your chart. Include at least two adverbials that tell time, place, manner or cause (for example: during the storm, suddenly, because of the attack, with desperate effort). Mention one fear or value about family."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Sentence starters: This episode is a turning point because ___. Before it, Percy ___. During the storm, ___ (page ___). Because ___, Percy ___. As a result, the adventure ___."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in explaining plot structure and adding detail with adverbials. Language focus: sequence and cause-effect connectors; adverbials of time, place, manner and cause.","sayAsk":"Have students rehearse aloud with a partner first: Tell your partner what happened before, during and after. Frames: Before this episode, ___. During the storm, ___. Because of the attack, ___. As a result, ___. Model expanding a sentence: Percy fights. Percy fights bravely during the attack because he wants to protect Grover. Invite planning in a home language, then writing in English.","watchFor":"If students write only a retelling, then prompt: How does this episode change what comes next? If students use no adverbials, then prompt: Add when, where, how or why to this sentence. Success: students state the ordinary world, what changes, and what the change launches, with two cited details and added adverbials."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Explaining structure","tryThis":"Give a before and after t-chart headed Ordinary world and New world. Have students fill in one detail for each, then join them in one sentence with because or so."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: Plot structure and theme","tryThis":"Ask students to explain how this episode also develops a theme about family and protection, and to find one earlier moment (Lesson 8) that this turning point echoes or reverses."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students summarize the turning point and its impact on Percy and connect it to the Performance Task skill.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-reflect","title":"Reflect: A Turning Point and Its Impact","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.5"],"routine":"Reflection","blocks":[{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"In Shared Stories, Shared Lessons, you will trace a turning point in a plot and explain its impact on a character. Today you practiced exactly that with Percy."},{"type":"directions","text":"Complete the template: The turning point on pp. 37–43 is ___. Before it, Percy's world was ___. After it, Percy ___. One fear or value about family shown in these pages is ___."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The turning point on pp. 37–43 is when Grover's cloven hooves show that the impossible is real. Before it, Percy's world was school troubles and a hard home life. After it, Percy has to leave his ordinary life behind and start an adventure. One value about family shown in these pages is that Percy wants to protect the people he cares about."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Collect the templates as an exit check. Look for a named event, a before and after contrast, and a family fear or value.
